newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Moslem rebels kill seven women in Algeria - paper.
newsitem.headline: Moslem rebels kill seven women in Algeria - paper.

text.p: Moslem guerrillas have killed seven women villagers by slashing their throats, an Algerian newspaper reported on Sunday.

La Tribune said the attack took place on Friday in Ouzrai in Medea province 70 kms (43 miles) southwest of the capital Algiers, when more than 40 rebels besieged the village with a list of people they wanted to assassinate.
"All the village's men fled and took refuge in the neighbouring forest," it said, adding that the assailants dragged the women from their homes and cut their throats.
Two days earlier about 30 guerrillas entered nearby Ouled Antar, hacking to death 32 people including 16 women and a 14-year-old boy, El Watan newspaper reported on Saturday.

More than 400 people have been killed in massacres and bombings in the past three months, mostly in Algiers and neighbouring towns. About 60,000 people have died since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.

La Tribune also reported that eight Moslem rebels were killed by a bomb they were trying to plant on Wednesday under a railway line near Tadmait village in Tizi-ouzou province 90 km (56 miles) southeast of Algiers.
According to a poll by the Arab-language daily al-Khabar, more than 52 percent of Algerians said they felt unsafe while 35.8 percent thought security was only partial.
"Despite this, 55.8 percent of Algerians see that the Algerian crisis will end soon, while 31.4 percent believe the end is still far off," the paper said.

More than 78 percent of those polled said they would vote in June 5 parliamentary elections, 14.3 percent said they would stay away, 6.7 percent declined to respond, and 55.3 percent believed the elections would be fair.
The authorities have set up an independent committee to supervise the polls and invited foreign observers.

Several politicians on Sunday hailed the appointment of Salah Boubnider, an outspoken former army colonel, to head the committee, saying he was a respected personality who could denounce any suspected foul play.
Algeria has had no parliament since 1992 when the election was cancelled.
